clue.text: Evidence of stoicism that may be under one's nose

definitions.meaning: a show of resolute self-control in adversity

definitions.text: that may be under one's nose
definitions.meaning: read literally, the part of the face just beneath the nose, held rigid

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes refusing to show emotion in adversity, a classic sign of stoic composure.

clue.text: Unexpectedly held up, son kept complaining

parts.note: to nag is to keep complaining at someone

explanation.surface: A son delayed by something who grumbles about it the whole time.
explanation.definitionFit: Something snagged is caught on an obstacle, so it is held up when nobody expected it.

clue.text: Latin thereby framed by lips of actor

indicators.note: the answer sits within the phrase, enclosed by its outer letters as though in a frame

explanation.surface: A Latin phrase being shaped by an actor's mouth as he delivers it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'framed by' marks the answer as hiding inside 'lips of actor', with only the L and R trimmed off the ends.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin tag means by that very fact, a formal way of saying thereby.

clue.text: Love fine fabric interlaced with gold

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads
lamé is a fabric woven with gold or silver threads

explanation.surface: A lover's gift of a fine cloth shot through with gold thread.
explanation.definitionFit: An old flame is a sweetheart, so the word stands for a person one loves.

clue.text: New cure put off may be a deflating experience

indicators.note: off in the sense of gone wrong or askew, telling us to rearrange these letters

explanation.surface: Delaying a new remedy might leave the patient feeling let down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' signals an anagram of N (new) with CURE PUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A puncture lets the air out of a tyre, literally an experience that deflates it.

clue.text: One feasting, keeping a Sunday — this one?

definitions.text: One feasting, keeping a Sunday — this one?

indicators.note: one word keeping another holds it inside, so the abbreviation goes within the feaster

parts.note: someone who feasts is an eater

explanation.surface: A diner tucking in on a holy Sunday, wondering which festival it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' puts S inside EATER; the whole clue also defines, since this Sunday is famous for feasting after Lent.
explanation.definitionFit: The festival is a Sunday in spring on which Christians traditionally feast after the Lenten fast.

clue.text: One carrying bombs to be thrown into street and river

indicators.note: one word placed into another goes inside it

parts.note: a lane is a narrow street
to cast is to throw, as with a line

explanation.surface: A bomber crew's deadly cargo about to be hurled into the street and river below.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' is a link and 'into' the container signal. The Avro Lancaster was Britain's best-known Second World War heavy bomber, so 'One' is not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lancaster was a heavy bomber aircraft, built to carry bombs over enemy territory.

clue.text: Special dish almost getting legal protection

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of the word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: a patent legally protects an invention

explanation.surface: An inventor's novel dish very nearly secures its patent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the final T from PATENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A paten is the plate used for the bread at Communion, a dish with a special sacred purpose.

clue.text: English composer writing part for violin

definitions.meaning: Frank ... was an English composer and the teacher of Benjamin Britten
the small upright piece of wood that holds a violin's strings away from its body

explanation.surface: An English composer scoring a passage for the violin section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'writing' is a link; 'part' looks like a musical part to play but means a physical component of the instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: a named English composer and the raised support over which violin strings pass.

clue.text: Give up smoking, say — horrible mark made by tar

parts.note: an AB, able seaman, is a sailor, as is a tar
a stain is an ugly mark

explanation.surface: Quitting cigarettes, because of the nasty yellow marks the tar leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tar' looks like part of the smoking picture but is crossword slang for a sailor, giving AB.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to refrain from something, and giving up smoking is one example of that.

clue.text: Politician wants military group to invade half of Serbia

indicators.note: one group invading another enters its territory, so these letters go inside
the first three of its six letters are taken

parts.note: NATO is the North Atlantic military alliance

explanation.surface: A politician demands that an alliance send troops into part of Serbia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wants' is a link; 'half of' takes the first three of Serbia's six letters, and 'to invade' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A senator is a member of a senate, a politician in an upper legislative chamber.

clue.text: From chief electrician, short is a bad mistake

indicators.note: short means cut off before the end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: the gaffer is the head electrician on a film set

explanation.surface: Anyone who wires a film set too short has made a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' drops the final R from GAFFER.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaffe is a social blunder, an embarrassing mistake.

clue.text: Ill-advised, and repent, having performed outdated surgery

indicators.note: badly advised, so the letters are wrongly arranged and must be put right

explanation.surface: A rash surgeon regrets an old-fashioned operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ill-advised' signals an anagram of AND REPENT; 'having' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To trepan is to bore a hole in the skull, an ancient surgical practice now long abandoned.

clue.text: Trim spar here?

parts.note: to dock is to cut short or trim
a yard is a spar on a ship's mast that carries a sail

explanation.surface: A question about where a ship's rigging might be cut to size.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a whole, the clue asks where a ship's spar would be trimmed: in a shipyard.
explanation.definitionFit: A dockyard is where ships are built and repaired, so masts and spars are worked on there.

clue.text: Anything vicar may be asked at baptism

definitions.meaning: a phrase meaning whatever you like, every possible thing

definitions.text: vicar may be asked at baptism
definitions.meaning: a christening priest might be told to go ahead and choose the child's name

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means anything at all you care to mention, and literally invites someone to give a name.

clue.text: Products all from same place in firm

definitions.meaning: a group of products or performers all coming from a single company or source

explanation.surface: Goods all made in one factory sold by one company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link; 'firm' looks like a company, but it means steady.
explanation.definitionFit: A stable is a group of things from one owner, and stable as an adjective means firm and secure.

clue.text: Saved, having experienced the Second Coming?

definitions.meaning: describing an evangelical Christian who has had a conversion experience
read literally, having arrived into the world for a second time

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a person converted to evangelical faith, saved, and literally someone delivered into the world twice.

clue.text: Gripe awfully over a measure of acidity in inscription

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over, above, the rest
awfully suggests the letters of the word are in a terrible mess

parts.note: pH is the scale measuring acidity

explanation.surface: Someone complaining bitterly about an acidity reading on a carved plaque.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awfully' signals an anagram of GRIPE, giving EPIGR, which goes 'over' A and PH in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An epigraph is an inscription carved on a building or statue, or a quotation at a book's head.

clue.text: Singers start to chant name of ancient god

indicators.note: the start of the next word means its first letter only

parts.note: Horus is the falcon-headed god of ancient Egypt

explanation.surface: A choir begins chanting the name of an old Egyptian deity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start to' takes C from 'chant'.
explanation.definitionFit: A chorus is a body of singers performing together.

clue.text: Sort of oil for wheel? Yes and no

definitions.meaning: a vegetable oil once used as a laxative
a small swivelling wheel fitted under furniture

explanation.surface: Asking whether a particular oil suits a squeaky wheel, and getting a mixed answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' and 'Yes and no' link the two senses: the oil is no lubricant for wheels, yet the same word does name a small wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: Castor is a medicinal oil and also a small pivoting wheel on a chair or trolley.

clue.text: Food God gave Adam

parts.note: a cut of pork, and in Genesis God made Eve from a rib taken from Adam, one he could spare

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a pork cut, and Genesis has Eve fashioned from a surplus bone of the first man.

clue.text: Poem boy found in pile of merchandise

indicators.note: something found in another lies inside it

parts.note: a bale is a large bundle of goods
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A poem about a boy discovered amid a heap of stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' is the container signal; 'Poem' is a ballade, a French verse form, not the more familiar ballad.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballade is a verse form of three stanzas and an envoi, a type of poem.

clue.text: Winger is seen in the flesh

indicators.note: something seen in another appears inside it

parts.note: skin is the flesh's outer covering

explanation.surface: A winger spotted in person rather than on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' suggests a footballer but is crossword shorthand for a bird; 'seen in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The siskin is a small finch, and a winger is crossword shorthand for a bird.

clue.text: Covering more ground, studying philosophy originally at university

indicators.note: originally means at the origin, so each word gives its first letter

parts.note: Reading is an English university town

explanation.surface: A student broadening their horizons by reading philosophy at college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' takes S and P from 'studying philosophy'; 'at' is a link. 'studying' wants to be READING, but that comes from 'university'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something spreading extends itself over a wider area, covering more ground.

clue.text: Crowds lifeboats

definitions.meaning: simple floating platforms used to escape a sinking ship

explanation.definitionFit: A raft is a great number of something, and rafts are also makeshift craft for survivors at sea.

clue.text: Pounds added on to fine for Scottish affray

indicators.note: one piece added on to another follows it

parts.note: braw is the Scots word for fine
L is the abbreviation for pounds, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A fine for a Scottish street fight with more money on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'added on to' puts L after BRAW. 'fine' looks like a penalty but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: An affray is a public fight, and a brawl is a rough noisy fight.

clue.text: Heartless barrister that's following this?

indicators.note: without its heart, only the first and last letters of the word remain

parts.note: i.e. stands for id est, that is
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

explanation.surface: A callous lawyer going along with his instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' keeps B and R from 'barrister'. The whole clue also defines: a barrister follows his written instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief is the written case a barrister is given and argues, so it is what he follows.

clue.text: No rush to get this ticket?

definitions.text: No rush to get this ticket?

parts.words: No rush to get this ticket?
parts.note: a cheaper fare valid only outside busy commuting hours, so the traveller avoids the rush hour

explanation.definitionFit: The term names a cheaper travel ticket for times outside the rush hour.

clue.text: He outwitted robbers and cut short excuse in court — a clever chap

indicators.note: cut short means the final letter is removed

parts.note: an alibi is a defendant's excuse of being elsewhere
a BA, a Bachelor of Arts graduate, is a learned person

explanation.surface: Someone who foiled thieves and gave a brief excuse before the judge, a smart fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' drops the final I of ALIBI; 'and' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Arabian Nights tale, Ali Baba foils the forty thieves with his slave girl Morgiana's help.

clue.text: Don't commit oneself to pin down criminal

definitions.meaning: decline to take sides in a dispute
read literally, to sit on a receiver of stolen goods and hold him down

explanation.surface: Advice to stay neutral, then a scene of grabbing a crook.
explanation.walkthrough: A fence is a dealer in stolen goods, and to sit on someone is to restrain them.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means staying neutral, and read literally pins down a receiver of stolen goods.
